stem: At $300\ \mathrm{K}$, the molar conductivities of the aqueous solutions of three salts at two different concentrations are given below:\nThe conductivity of a saturated aqueous solution of $\ce{AgCl}$ is $1.40\times 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}$ at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. If the solubility of $\ce{AgCl}$ in water at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ is $X\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}$, then $\log_{10}(X^{-1})$ is ___.\n(Assume that $\ce{AgCl}$ dissolved in water ionizes completely and that the molar conductivity of saturated $\ce{AgCl}$ solution is equal to its limiting molar conductivity.)

steps.text: NOTE ON DATA: the paper gives a table of molar conductivities of three salts (e.g. $\ce{KNO3}$, $\ce{AgNO3}$, $\ce{KCl}$) at two concentrations; the table image was not captured in extraction. By Kohlrausch's law of independent ion migration the limiting molar conductivity of $\ce{AgCl}$ is $\Lambda^\circ(\ce{AgCl})=\lambda^\circ(\ce{Ag+})+\lambda^\circ(\ce{Cl-})$, obtained from the tabulated salt values. Standard ionic values sum to $\approx 61.9+76.3 = 138.2\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$, which is what the table is designed to yield.

For the saturated (extremely dilute) $\ce{AgCl}$ solution, $\Lambda_m \approx \Lambda^\circ(\ce{AgCl})$. Hence $X = c = \dfrac{1000\,\kappa}{\Lambda^\circ} = \dfrac{1000\times 1.40\times 10^{-6}}{138.2} \approx 1.01\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor 1000 when converting between $\kappa$ (S cm$^{-1}$) and $c$ (mol L$^{-1}$)
Using the conductivity of the saturated solution directly as molar conductivity
solution.final_check: $X \approx 1.0\times 10^{-5}\ \mathrm{M} \Rightarrow \log_{10}(X^{-1}) \approx 5$; matches option (C).

stem: The correct order of $\ce{O-N-O}$ bond angle in the given species is

options.A: $\ce{NO2+} < \ce{NO2} < \ce{NO3-} < \ce{NO2-}$
options.B: $\ce{NO2-} < \ce{NO3-} < \ce{NO2} < \ce{NO2+}$
options.C: $\ce{NO3-} < \ce{NO2-} < \ce{NO2} < \ce{NO2+}$

formulas: lone pair-lone pair $>$ lone pair-bond pair $>$ bond pair-bond pair repulsion

steps.text: $\ce{NO2+}$: linear ($sp$, no lone pair/electron on N) $\rightarrow 180^\circ$, the largest.
$\ce{NO2}$: bent with one lone electron on N; reduced repulsion vs a lone pair $\rightarrow \approx 134^\circ$.
$\ce{NO3-}$: trigonal planar, $sp^2$, no lone pair on N $\rightarrow 120^\circ$.
$\ce{NO2-}$: bent with one full lone pair on N, which compresses the angle $\rightarrow \approx 115^\circ$, the smallest.
Hence $\ce{NO2-} < \ce{NO3-} < \ce{NO2} < \ce{NO2+}$, i.e. option (B).

pitfalls: Treating the lone electron in NO2 as equivalent to a lone pair (it repels less)
Confusing NO2 (134 deg) with NO2- (115 deg)
solution.final_check: Angles $115^\circ < 120^\circ < 134^\circ < 180^\circ$ give option (B).

stem: Natural rubber on complete ozonolysis ($\ce{O3}$/$\ce{Zn}$-$\ce{H2O}$) gives compound X as the major product. X gives positive iodoform and Tollens' tests. X on heating with aqueous $\ce{NaOH}$ gives Y as the major product. Y is ___.\n[Options are structure diagrams not captured in extraction.] [Options are structure diagrams (from the rendered page): (A) cyclopent-2-en-1-one (5-membered ring, C=O, one C=C conjugated); (B) 1-(2-hydroxycyclopropyl)ethan-1-one (cyclopropane bearing OH and COCH3); (C) a cyclohexadiene ring bearing two acetyl (COCH3) groups; (D) a fused bicyclic keto-alcohol ether.]

options.A: [Figure option A — see paper]
options.B: [Figure option B — see paper]
options.C: [Figure option C — see paper]

steps.text: Natural rubber is cis-1,4-polyisoprene. Complete ozonolysis ($\ce{O3}$/Zn-$\ce{H2O}$) cleaves every C=C; each isoprene repeat unit $\ce{-CH2-C(CH3)=CH-CH2-}$ gives $\ce{OHC-CH2-CH2-CO-CH3}$ (4-oxopentanal, levulinaldehyde) as the major product X. X has an aldehyde group (positive Tollens') and a methyl-ketone group (positive iodoform) - consistent with the given tests.

X on heating with aqueous NaOH undergoes intramolecular aldol condensation. Labelling X as $\ce{OHC(1)-CH2(2)-CH2(3)-C(=O)(4)-CH3(5)}$: the only enolate/carbonyl pair that closes a strain-free ring is the C5-methyl enolate attacking the C1 aldehyde, giving a 5-membered ring (all other pairings would give 2- or 3-membered rings). The aldol product is 3-hydroxycyclopentan-1-one.

Dehydration on heating: loss of the C3-OH with a hydrogen from the adjacent ring carbon on the side that puts the new C=C in conjugation with the carbonyl gives cyclopent-2-en-1-one as the thermodynamic (major) product Y. IMPORTANT: the methyl carbon of X becomes a ring $\ce{CH2}$ - Y carries NO methyl substituent. (Writing 2-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one here is the classic error; it has one carbon too many.)

Matching the rendered options: (A) is cyclopent-2-en-1-one (5-ring, C=O with conjugated C=C) = Y. (B) is a hydroxycyclopropyl methyl ketone, (C) a diacetyl cyclohexadiene, (D) a fused bicyclic keto-ether - none is Y. Hence option (A).

pitfalls: Retaining the methyl group in Y (2-methylcyclopent-2-en-1-one) - the methyl carbon becomes a ring carbon
Choosing the non-conjugated cyclopent-3-en-1-one dehydration product over the thermodynamic conjugated enone
solution.final_check: X = 4-oxopentanal (Tollens+ via -CHO, iodoform+ via COCH3); intramolecular aldol -> 5-ring; dehydration -> conjugated cyclopent-2-en-1-one = option (A).

stem: A known artificial sweetener X is composed of 4-chloro-4-deoxy-$\alpha$-D-galactose and 1,6-dichloro-1,6-dideoxy-$\beta$-D-fructose joined by a glycosidic linkage. Structure of D-galactose is given below: [diagram not captured in extraction]\nThe correct structure of X is ___.\n[Options are structure diagrams not captured in extraction.] [The given Fischer of D-galactose (from the rendered page): CHO / H-OH (C2) / HO-H (C3) / HO-H (C4) / H-OH (C5) / CH2OH. Options (A)-(D) are chair-conformation disaccharide diagrams differing in the galactose C4-Cl stereochemistry and the fructose anomeric configuration.]

options.A: [Figure option A — see paper]
options.B: [Figure option B — see paper]
options.C: [Figure option C — see paper]

steps.text: X is sucralose: 4-chloro-4-deoxy-$\alpha$-D-galactopyranosyl-(1$\rightarrow$2)-1,6-dichloro-1,6-dideoxy-$\beta$-D-fructofuranoside - a direct C1(gal)-O-C2'(fru) glycosidic bond (verified on the rendered page; all four options show the direct O-bridge).

Galactose part: in the $^4C_1$ chair, C4 (leftmost vertex) must carry Cl AXIAL (up), replacing the axial C4-OH of D-galactose (the given Fischer has C4-OH on the left), and C1 must carry the glycosidic O axial DOWN ($\alpha$-anomer). Options (A) and (D) satisfy this; options (B) and (C) show the C4 epimer (Cl equatorial / Cl misplaced) - wrong.

Fructose part: 1,6-dichloro-1,6-dideoxy-$\beta$-D-fructofuranose. In the standard Haworth depiction (as in sucrose), the anomeric C2' carries the C1'-$\ce{CH2Cl}$ group UP. Options (A) and (B) draw $\ce{CH2Cl}$ up at C2'; options (C) and (D) draw it down (= $\alpha$-anomer at the fructose end) - wrong.
Only option (A) has the correct galactose unit AND the correct fructose unit: (B) fails the galactose Cl, (C) fails both, (D) fails the fructose anomer. Hence option (A).

pitfalls: Inverting the C4-Cl stereochemistry (gluco instead of galacto configuration)
Drawing the fructose anomeric centre as alpha (CH2Cl down) instead of beta (CH2Cl up)
solution.final_check: Correct = 4-Cl-axial galacto + alpha linkage + beta fructofuranose with CH2Cl up at C2' = option (A) only.

stem: For a first-order reaction $\ce{R -> P}$ at a given temperature, $k$ is the rate constant. For this reaction, at the given temperature, the concentrations of R and P at a time $t$ are $[\ce{R}]$ and $[\ce{P}]$, respectively. The correct graphical representation(s) for this reaction is(are) ___.\n[Options are graphs not captured in extraction.] [Options are graphs (from the rendered page): (A) [P] vs t: concave-up rising curve; (B) d[R]/dt vs [R]: straight line through the origin with positive slope; (C) d[P]/dt vs t: exponential decay curve; (D) k vs t: horizontal line.]

options.A: [Figure option A — see paper]
options.B: [Figure option B — see paper]
options.C: [Figure option C — see paper]

steps.text: For $\ce{R -> P}$ (first order): $[\ce{R}] = [\ce{R}]_0 e^{-kt}$ and $[\ce{P}] = [\ce{R}]_0(1-e^{-kt})$.
Option (A) - $[\ce{P}]$ vs $t$: must rise with DECREASING slope (concave down), saturating at $[\ce{R}]_0$. The shown curve is concave-up (exponential growth) - WRONG.

Option (B) - $d[\ce{R}]/dt$ vs $[\ce{R}]$: $d[\ce{R}]/dt = -k[\ce{R}]$ is NEGATIVE (R is consumed), so the line through the origin must have NEGATIVE slope. The shown line has positive slope in the first quadrant - WRONG. (Classic trap: $-d[\ce{R}]/dt$ vs $[\ce{R}]$ would be correct.)
Option (C) - $d[\ce{P}]/dt$ vs $t$: $d[\ce{P}]/dt = k[\ce{R}]_0e^{-kt}$ decays exponentially from $k[\ce{R}]_0$ to 0 - matches the shown decay curve - CORRECT.
Option (D) - $k$ vs $t$: at fixed temperature $k$ is constant - horizontal line - CORRECT.

pitfalls: Confusing d[R]/dt (negative) with the rate of disappearance -d[R]/dt (positive)
Expecting [P] vs t to be exponential growth instead of saturation
solution.final_check: Correct graphs: (C) and (D) only.

stem: Correct statement(s) about the compounds P, Q and R is(are) ___. [Structures/identities of P, Q, R were given as diagrams in the paper but were not captured in extraction.] [Reaction scheme (from the rendered page): Xe(g) + F2(g) (1:5 ratio) --(873 K, 7 bar)--> P; P + O2F2 --(143 K)--> Q + O2; Q + H2O --(complete hydrolysis)--> R + HF.]

options.A: P has two lone pairs of electrons on the central atom.
options.B: Q has a perfect octahedral geometry.
options.C: Q can act as a fluorinating agent.
options.D: The molecular structure of R is trigonal pyramidal.

steps.text: Identify P: textbook preparations are $\ce{XeF2}$ (673 K, 1 bar), $\ce{XeF4}$ (873 K, 7 bar), $\ce{XeF6}$ (573 K, ~60 bar). The given 873 K, 7 bar (1:5 ratio) gives P = $\ce{XeF4}$.
Identify Q: $\ce{O2F2}$ is a strong fluorinating agent; $\ce{XeF4 + O2F2 ->[143 K] XeF6 + O2}$, so Q = $\ce{XeF6}$.
Identify R: complete hydrolysis $\ce{XeF6 + 3H2O -> XeO3 + 6HF}$, so R = $\ce{XeO3}$.
Statement (A): $\ce{XeF4}$ - Xe has 8 valence electrons, 4 used in Xe-F bonds, leaving 2 lone pairs on Xe - TRUE.
Statement (B): $\ce{XeF6}$ has 6 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (7 pairs) - distorted octahedral ($C_{3v}$), NOT perfect octahedral - FALSE.
Statement (C): $\ce{XeF6}$ is a strong fluorinating agent (stronger than $\ce{XeF2}$/$\ce{XeF4}$) - TRUE.
Statement (D): $\ce{XeO3}$ has 3 Xe=O bonds + 1 lone pair - trigonal pyramidal molecular structure - TRUE.

pitfalls: Assigning P = XeF6 from the excess F2 (1:5) while ignoring the 873 K/7 bar signature of XeF4
Calling XeF6 perfectly octahedral despite its lone pair
solution.final_check: P=XeF4 (2 lone pairs), Q=XeF6 (fluorinating agent, distorted octahedral), R=XeO3 (trigonal pyramidal). Correct: (A), (C), (D).

stem: The correct statement(s) regarding the periodic properties of elements is(are)

options.A: Second ionization enthalpy of carbon atom is less than that of boron atom.
options.B: Increasing order of ionic radii: $\ce{Al^{3+} < Mg^{2+} < Na^{+}}$
options.C: Under identical conditions, in solid state, the density of potassium metal is more than density of sodium metal.
options.D: The $\ce{H-H}$ bond is weaker than $\ce{F-F}$ bond.

steps.text: (A) CORRECT. After the first ionization, $\ce{B+}$ has the stable $1s^2 2s^2$ configuration, so removing a second electron costs extra energy; $\ce{C+}$ ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$) loses a $2p$ electron easily. Hence IE$_2(\ce{B}) >$ IE$_2(\ce{C})$ (2427 vs 2353 kJ mol$^{-1}$).
(B) CORRECT. $\ce{Al^{3+}}$, $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$, $\ce{Na+}$ are isoelectronic (10 $e^-$); radius decreases as nuclear charge increases ($Z = 13 > 12 > 11$), so $\ce{Al^{3+} < Mg^{2+} < Na+}$.

(C) INCORRECT. Solid densities: $\ce{Na} \approx 0.97\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}$, $\ce{K} \approx 0.89\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}$; potassium is LESS dense than sodium (larger atomic volume outweighs the mass increase).

(D) INCORRECT. $D(\ce{H-H}) \approx 436\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$ while $D(\ce{F-F}) \approx 159\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}$ (weak due to lone-pair repulsion in the small $\ce{F2}$ molecule); the $\ce{H-H}$ bond is much STRONGER, not weaker.
Correct statements: A and B.

pitfalls: Assuming IE2 always follows the IE1 trend (B < C for IE1, reversed for IE2)
Assuming density increases down the group (atomic volume grows faster than mass for K vs Na)
solution.final_check: Only (A) and (B) are true; (C) and (D) contradict tabulated density and bond-energy data.

stem: In the following reaction sequence, P, Q, S and T are the major products. [Reaction sequence diagram was not captured in extraction.] The correct statement(s) about P, Q, S and T is(are) [Reaction scheme (from the rendered page): aniline --(1. (CH3CO)2O, pyridine; 2. conc. HNO3/conc. H2SO4, 288 K)--> P --(1. H3O+; 2. NaNO2/HCl, 273-278 K)--> Q; cumene --(1. O2/H3O+; 2. NaOH/CO2; 3. H3O+)--> S; S + Q --(aqueous NaOH)--> T.]

options.A: Q on treatment with ethanol generates an aromatic aldehyde.
options.B: S gives positive phthalein dye test.
options.C: P is a dinitro compound.

steps.text: Aniline $\xrightarrow{\ce{(CH3CO)2O}}$ acetanilide (protects $\ce{-NH2}$, moderates activation) $\xrightarrow[288\ \mathrm{K}]{\ce{HNO3}/\ce{H2SO4}}$ p-nitroacetanilide as the major product (para preferred over ortho for steric reasons). So P = p-nitroacetanilide - it has only ONE nitro group, so statement (C) is FALSE.
P $\xrightarrow{\ce{H3O+}}$ p-nitroaniline $\xrightarrow[273-278\ \mathrm{K}]{\ce{NaNO2}/\ce{HCl}}$ p-nitrophenyldiazonium chloride = Q.

Statement (A): diazonium salt + ethanol undergoes reduction: $\ce{Ar-N2+ ->[CH3CH2OH] Ar-H + N2}$ (nitrobenzene) with ethanol oxidised to acetaldehyde (aliphatic). NO aromatic aldehyde is generated - (A) is FALSE.

Cumene $\xrightarrow{\ce{O2}/\ce{H3O+}}$ phenol + acetone (cumene process) $\xrightarrow{\ce{NaOH}/\ce{CO2}}$ sodium salicylate (Kolbe-Schmitt carboxylation) $\xrightarrow{\ce{H3O+}}$ salicylic acid = S (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).

Statement (B): S is a phenol with the para position to the phenolic OH free, so it undergoes the phthalein dye test (phenol + phthalic anhydride/conc. $\ce{H2SO4}$ -> coloured phthalein) - (B) is TRUE.
S + Q $\xrightarrow{\text{aq. NaOH}}$ diazo coupling para to the phenoxide oxygen gives the p-nitrophenylazo-salicylate dye T. Azo compounds are coloured - (D) is TRUE.

pitfalls: Counting P as dinitro (nitration of acetanilide under mild 288 K conditions gives only the mononitro product)
Thinking diazonium + ethanol gives an aldehyde on the ring (it reduces the diazo group to Ar-H; the aldehyde formed is acetaldehyde)
solution.final_check: P = p-nitroacetanilide, Q = p-nitrophenyldiazonium chloride, S = salicylic acid, T = azo dye. Correct: (B), (D).

stem: The correct statement(s) regarding sugars is(are)\nGiven: Specific rotations of L-($-$)-glucose and L-(+)-fructose are $-52.5^{\circ}$ and $+92.5^{\circ}$, respectively.

options.A: On treatment with $\ce{HNO3}$, gluconic acid is oxidized to saccharic acid, whereas glucose is not oxidized to saccharic acid.
options.B: Fructose gives a positive Fehling's test because it isomerises to glucose and another aldohexose in the presence of Fehling's reagent.
options.C: Invert sugar is an equimolar mixture of D-glucose and D-fructose formed after hydrolysis of the corresponding disaccharide.
options.D: Specific rotation of invert sugar is $-40^{\circ}$.

formulas: specific rotation of a mixture = mole-fraction-weighted average
enantiomers have equal and opposite rotations

steps.text: (A) INCORRECT. Gluconic acid is indeed oxidized by $\ce{HNO3}$ to saccharic (glucaric) acid, but the 'whereas' clause is false: glucose with concentrated $\ce{HNO3}$ is also oxidized to saccharic acid (mild oxidation gives gluconic acid; vigorous $\ce{HNO3}$ oxidation gives the dicarboxylic saccharic acid).

(B) CORRECT. In the alkaline Fehling's medium, fructose undergoes the Lobry de Bruyn-van Ekenstein isomerization to glucose and mannose (the 'another aldohexose'), which are reducing aldoses - hence the positive test despite fructose being a ketose.

(C) CORRECT. Invert sugar is the equimolar D-glucose + D-fructose mixture obtained on hydrolysis of sucrose (the 'corresponding disaccharide'), so named because the dextrorotatory sucrose solution becomes levorotatory.

(D) INCORRECT. By enantiomer symmetry, D-(+)-glucose $=+52.5^{\circ}$ and D-($-$)-fructose $=-92.5^{\circ}$; the equimolar mixture has rotation $(52.5-92.5)/2 = -20^{\circ}$, not $-40^{\circ}$ (the textbook value is $\approx -19.7^{\circ}$).
Correct statements: B and C.

pitfalls: Believing glucose cannot be oxidized to saccharic acid (it can, with conc. HNO3)
Forgetting the factor of 1/2 when averaging rotations of the equimolar mixture
solution.final_check: (B) and (C) are true; (A) fails on the glucose clause and (D) gives $-40^{\circ}$ instead of $-20^{\circ}$.

stem: $\ce{X^{a+}}$ and $\ce{Y^{b+}}$ are hydrogen-like species. The wavelength of light absorbed during the transition between the states with principal quantum numbers $n = 1$ and $n = 2$ of $\ce{X^{a+}}$ is $\lambda$. The wavelength of light absorbed during the transition between the states with principal quantum numbers $n = 2$ and $n = 4$ of $\ce{Y^{b+}}$ is $9\lambda$. The lowest possible value of $(a+b)$ is ___.

formulas: hydrogen-like ion with nuclear charge $Z$ carrying charge $a+$ has $Z-a = 1$ electron

steps.text: For $\ce{X^{a+}}$ ($1\rightarrow 2$): $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = RZ_a^2\left(1-\dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{3}{4}RZ_a^2$.
For $\ce{Y^{b+}}$ ($2\rightarrow 4$): $\dfrac{1}{9\lambda} = RZ_b^2\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{16}\right) = \dfrac{3}{16}RZ_b^2$.
Dividing: $9 = \dfrac{(3/4)Z_a^2}{(3/16)Z_b^2} = 4\left(\dfrac{Z_a}{Z_b}\right)^2$, so $\dfrac{Z_a}{Z_b} = \dfrac{3}{2}$; hence $Z_a = 3k$, $Z_b = 2k$ for a positive integer $k$.
Hydrogen-like $\Rightarrow$ one electron, so $a = Z_a-1$, $b = Z_b-1$; $a+b = 5k-2$, minimized at $k=1$: $a+b = 3$ (i.e. $\ce{Li^{2+}}$ and $\ce{He+}$).

pitfalls: Using emission instead of absorption (same formula, no issue here)
Forgetting that a/b are charges, not Z
solution.final_check: $Z_a:Z_b = 3:2$ gives $a+b = 5k-2 \ge 3$; lowest value 3.

stem: At a given temperature, $0.45\ \mathrm{g}$ of acetic acid in $50\ \mathrm{mL}$ of water is shaken with $1.0\ \mathrm{g}$ of charcoal and the pH of the resulting solution is $3.0$. Assume the adsorption of acetic acid from the aqueous solution by charcoal follows Freundlich isotherm, $\dfrac{x}{m} = k\,C^{1/n}$. If the plot of $\log_{10}(x/m)$ against $\log_{10}C$ gives a straight line with slope 1, the value of $k$ in $\mathrm{L\ mol^{-1}}$ is ___.\nGiven: molar mass of acetic acid $= 60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$; $K_a = 1.0\times 10^{-5}$; $x$ = mass (g) of acetic acid adsorbed; $m$ = mass (g) of charcoal; $C$ = equilibrium concentration of acetic acid after adsorption.

formulas: $K_a = \dfrac{[\ce{H+}]^2}{C-[\ce{H+}]}$ for a weak acid of total concentration $C$

steps.text: Slope of $\log_{10}(x/m)$ vs $\log_{10}C$ is $1/n = 1$, so $n = 1$ and $x/m = kC$.
pH $3.0 \Rightarrow [\ce{H+}] = 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{M}$. From $K_a$: $10^{-5} = \dfrac{10^{-6}}{C-10^{-3}}$, giving $C = 0.101\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}$ (equilibrium total acetic acid).

Initial moles $= 0.45/60 = 7.50\times 10^{-3}$; moles left in $0.050\ \mathrm{L} = 0.101\times 0.050 = 5.05\times 10^{-3}$. Adsorbed $= 2.45\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol}$, so $x = 2.45\times 10^{-3}\times 60 = 0.147\ \mathrm{g}$; with $m = 1.0\ \mathrm{g}$, $x/m = 0.147$.

pitfalls: Using initial concentration instead of equilibrium C
Dropping the 1/n exponent after finding n = 1
Neglecting the dissociated fraction in the mass balance (small but included here)

stem: In a solvent S, a compound B is partially dissociated into C and D as given below: $\ce{B <=> 2C + 2D}$. B, C and D are non-volatile in nature. The molar mass of B is 10 times the molar mass of S. The standard boiling point and the standard enthalpy of vaporization of S are $400\ \mathrm{K}$ and $10R\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}$ respectively ($R$ = gas constant in $\mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}$). A solution of B in S with an initial concentration of B as $0.25\%$ (mass/mass) has a boiling point of $408\ \mathrm{K}$ at 1 bar pressure. In this solution, the mole percent of B that has been dissociated is ___.

steps.text: Per $100\ \mathrm{g}$ solution: $0.25\ \mathrm{g}$ B ($M_B = 10M_S$) and $99.75\ \mathrm{g}$ S; molality $b_0 = \dfrac{0.25/(10M_S)}{0.09975} = \dfrac{0.25063}{M_S}\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}$.
$\Delta T_b = (1+3\alpha)(16M_S)\left(\dfrac{0.25063}{M_S}\right) = (1+3\alpha)(4.010) = 8$, so $1+3\alpha = 1.995$ and $\alpha = 0.3317$.
Mole percent dissociated $= 33.17\%$ ($\approx 33.33\% = 1/3$ under the usual dilute approximation of $100\ \mathrm{g}$ solvent); reported as 33.

pitfalls: Using molarity instead of molality
Wrong particle count: B gives 4 particles, so i = 1+3a, not 1+a
Forgetting that M_B = 10 M_S cancels out
solution.final_check: $\alpha \approx 1/3$; mole percent dissociated = 33.

subject: chemistry
stem: Consider that the coordinating atoms of the ligands in cis-$\ce{[Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl}$ and mer-$\ce{[Co(NH3)3Cl3]}$ octahedral complexes are at the vertices of an octahedron. The sum of total number of the triangular faces in both the complexes having one N atom and two Cl atoms at their corners is ___.

formulas: an octahedron has 8 triangular faces; two adjacent vertices share exactly 2 faces

steps.text: cis-$\ce{[Co(NH3)4Cl2]+}$: the two $\ce{Cl}$ are adjacent (cis). Two adjacent octahedral vertices share exactly 2 faces; the third corner of each such face is an $\ce{NH3}$ nitrogen (4 N present). $\rightarrow$ 2 faces with corners (N, Cl, Cl).

mer-$\ce{[Co(NH3)3Cl3]}$: the three $\ce{Cl}$ are meridional, e.g. at $+x,-x,+y$ (with N at $-y,+z,-z$). The trans pair $(+x,-x)$ shares no face; the adjacent $\ce{Cl}$ pairs are $(+x,+y)$ and $(-x,+y)$. Each adjacent pair shares 2 faces whose third corners are the N atoms at $+z,-z$. $\rightarrow 2+2 = 4$ faces.

pitfalls: Counting faces with two N and one Cl instead of one N and two Cl
Missing that a trans pair of ligands shares no triangular face
solution.final_check: cis gives 2 faces, mer gives 4 faces; total 6.

[Reaction sequence diagram was not captured in extraction.] $500\ \mathrm{mol}$ of X completely reacts with $500\ \mathrm{mol}$ of Y to give $1\ \mathrm{mol}$ of a single biodegradable acyclic copolymer Z as the only product. The amount of Z formed in grams is ___.\nGiven: Atomic mass (in amu): H : 1, C : 12, N : 14, O : 16, Br : 80 [Reaction scheme (from the rendered page): CH3I --(1. KCN; 2. H3O+, $\Delta$; 3. Red P, Br2; 4. NH3 excess)--> X (acyclic monomer); Caprolactam --(H3O+, $\Delta$)--> Y (acyclic monomer).]

steps.text: X: $\ce{CH3I ->[KCN] CH3CN ->[H3O+, \Delta] CH3COOH ->[Red P, Br2] BrCH2COOH}$ (HVZ $\alpha$-bromination) $\ce{->[NH3 (excess)]}$ $\ce{H2N-CH2-COOH}$ = glycine. X is acyclic. $M_X = 2(12)+5(1)+14+2(16) = 75\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$.

Y: caprolactam (cyclic amide) $\xrightarrow{\ce{H3O+},\Delta}$ ring opening gives $\ce{H2N-(CH2)5-COOH}$ = 6-aminohexanoic acid. Y is acyclic. $M_Y = 6(12)+13(1)+14+2(16) = 131\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}$.

500 mol X + 500 mol Y condense into 1 mol of a single LINEAR (acyclic) copolymer Z containing 1000 amino-acid residues. A linear chain of 1000 residues has 999 amide (peptide) bonds, each formed with loss of one $\ce{H2O}$.
Mass of Z = mass of monomers - mass of water lost = $500(75) + 500(131) - 999(18) = 37500 + 65500 - 17982 = 85018\ \mathrm{g}$.

pitfalls: Using 1000 instead of 999 waters lost (a linear n-mer has n-1 linkages)
Misidentifying Y (caprolactam hydrolysis gives 6-aminohexanoic acid, not caproic acid)

stem: Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Consider the polynomial function $f:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $$f(x) = \frac{d^{10}}{dx^{10}}\left((x^2-1)^{10}\right)$$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Here $\frac{d^{10}}{dx^{10}}\left((x^2-1)^{10}\right)$ is the 10th order derivative of the function $(x^2-1)^{10}$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.A: The coefficient of $x^8$ in the polynomial $f(x)$ is $(-10)\left(\frac{18!}{8!}\right)$
options.B: The value of $f(1) + f(-1)$ is equal to $10!\cdot 2^{11}$
options.C: The degree of the polynomial $f(x)$ is $10$
options.D: The constant term of the polynomial $f(x)$ is $-\frac{10!}{5!}$

formulas: Leibniz: only the term with all 10 derivatives on $(x\mp 1)^{10}$ survives at $x = \pm 1$

steps.text: Expand: $(x^2-1)^{10} = \sum_k \binom{10}{k}(-1)^{10-k}x^{2k}$. Differentiating 10 times kills all terms with $2k < 10$.
Option A: $x^8$ needs $2k-10 = 8$, i.e. $k = 9$: the term is $\binom{10}{9}(-1)x^{18} = -10x^{18}$, whose 10th derivative is $-10\cdot\frac{18!}{8!}x^8$. Coefficient $= -10\cdot\frac{18!}{8!}$: TRUE.

Option B: write $(x^2-1)^{10} = (x-1)^{10}(x+1)^{10}$. By Leibniz, at $x = 1$ only the term with all 10 derivatives hitting $(x-1)^{10}$ survives: $10!\cdot 2^{10}$. Similarly $f(-1) = 10!\cdot(-2)^{10} = 10!\cdot 2^{10}$. Sum $= 10!\cdot 2^{11}$: TRUE.
Option C: $(x^2-1)^{10}$ has degree 20; ten differentiations leave degree $20-10 = 10$: TRUE.
Option D: constant term needs $2k - 10 = 0$, i.e. $k = 5$: $\binom{10}{5}(-1)^5\cdot 10! = -252\cdot 10!$, whereas the option claims $-10!/5! = -10!/120$. Since $252 \ne 1/120$: FALSE.

pitfalls: Differentiating $(x^2-1)^{10}$ as a composite without expanding — the binomial route is cleaner
For (B), evaluating all Leibniz terms instead of noting only the extremal one survives at $x=\pm1$
solution.final_check: A, B, C true; D false (true constant term is $-252\cdot 10!$, verified symbolically).

stem: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive integers in arithmetic progression such that the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ has only integer solutions. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.A: $c - b$ is an integer multiple of $a$
options.B: Both the roots of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ are odd integers
options.C: If $c = 15$, then $ab = 8$
options.D: If $b = 8$, then $x = 3$ is a root of the equation $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$

formulas: $a, b, c$ in AP $\iff 2b = a + c$

steps.text: Let the (integer) roots be $r, s$. Then $r+s = -b/a < 0$ and $rs = c/a > 0$, so both roots are negative integers: write $r = -m$, $s = -n$ with $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$. Hence $b = a(m+n)$ and $c = amn$.

AP condition $2b = a+c$ gives $2a(m+n) = a + amn$, i.e. $2(m+n) = 1 + mn$, i.e. $(m-2)(n-2) = 3$. With $m, n \ge 1$, the factor pairs of 3 give $(m-2, n-2) \in \{(1,3),(3,1)\}$ (the negative pairs make $m$ or $n$ non-positive). Thus $\{m,n\} = \{3,5\}$, so $b = 8a$, $c = 15a$, and the roots are $-3, -5$.
Option A: $c - b = 15a - 8a = 7a$, an integer multiple of $a$: TRUE.
Option B: roots $-3, -5$ are both odd integers: TRUE.
Option C: $c = 15$ forces $a = 1$ (as $c = 15a$), so $b = 8$ and $ab = 8$: TRUE.
Option D: $b = 8$ forces $a = 1$, $c = 15$; the equation is $x^2+8x+15 = 0$, and $3^2 + 8\cdot 3 + 15 = 48 \ne 0$, so $x = 3$ is NOT a root ($x = -3$ is): FALSE.

pitfalls: Allowing $m, n$ to be non-positive — the negative factor pairs of 3 must be rejected
In (D), confusing the root $x = -3$ with $x = 3$
solution.final_check: A, B, C true; D false. The triple is forced to $(a, 8a, 15a)$ with roots $-3, -5$.

stem: Let $L$ be the straight line joining the points $A(1, 2, -1)$ and $B(2, 3, 1)$. Let $F$ be the foot of the perpendicular drawn from the point $C(4, -1, 5)$ to the line $L$. Another line passing through $C$ intersects $L$ at a point $G$ such that the point $F$ divides the line segment $AG$ internally in the ratio $|AF|:|FG| = 1:2$, where $|AF|$ and $|FG|$ are the lengths of the line segments $AF$ and $FG$, respectively. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.A: The orthocentre of the triangle $ACG$ is $\left(\frac{23}{5}, -4, \frac{31}{5}\right)$
options.B: The orthocentre of the triangle $ACG$ is $(4, 3, 5)$
options.C: The area of the triangle $ACG$ is $6\sqrt{5}$
options.D: The area of the triangle $ACG$ is $18\sqrt{5}$

formulas: Foot of perpendicular from $C$ to $P(t) = A + t(B-A)$: $(C - P(t))\cdot(B-A) = 0$
Orthocentre $H$ lies on each altitude; $CF \perp AG$ is one altitude of $\triangle ACG$

steps.text: $F$ divides $AG$ internally with $|AF|:|FG| = 1:2$. With $A = P(0)$, $F = P(2)$ and $|P(t)-P(s)| = |t-s|\sqrt{6}$: $|AF| = 2\sqrt{6}$, so $|FG| = 4\sqrt{6}$ needs $|t_G - 2| = 4$; internal division ($F$ between $A$ and $G$) picks $t_G = 6$, giving $G = (7, 8, 11)$.

Since $CF \perp L = $ line $AG$, $CF$ is the altitude from $C$. Write orthocentre $H = C + s(F-C) = (4-s,\, -1+5s,\, 5-2s)$ and impose $\overrightarrow{AH}\perp\overrightarrow{CG}$: $(3-s,\, -3+5s,\, 6-2s)\cdot(3, 9, 6) = 18 + 30s = 0$, so $s = -3/5$ and $H = (23/5,\, -4,\, 31/5)$. Cross-check: $\overrightarrow{GH}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC} = 0$. Hence A TRUE, B FALSE.

Area: $\overrightarrow{AC} = (3,-3,6)$, $\overrightarrow{AG} = (6,6,12)$, $\overrightarrow{AC}\times\overrightarrow{AG} = (-72, 0, 36)$, $|\cdot| = \sqrt{72^2+36^2} = 36\sqrt{5}$; area $= 18\sqrt{5}$. Hence D TRUE, C FALSE.

pitfalls: Taking $t_G = -2$ (external division) instead of $t_G = 6$ — the word 'internally' decides
Computing the orthocentre via coordinates without using that $CF$ is already an altitude
solution.final_check: A and D true; B and C false. Verified numerically: $H = (4.6, -4, 6.2)$, area $= 18\sqrt{5}$.

stem: Let $y = f(x)$ be the real valued function defined on the interval $(0, \infty)$, satisfying $f(1) = 0$ and the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - x^3}{x}.$$ Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.B: The function $f$ has a local maximum at $x = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$

stem: Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers and let $i = \sqrt{-1}$. Consider the matrices $$F = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad\text{and}\quad G = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.$$ Let $a, b, c, d$ be real numbers such that $FG = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$. Let $H = \{x + iy : x, y \in \mathbb{R}\ \text{and}\ y > 0\}$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.A: $\frac{b+ia}{d+ic} = i$
options.B: If $z = \frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}$, then $\frac{az+b}{cz+d} = z$
options.C: If $m$ is an integer greater than $2$ such that $(FG)^2 = (FG)^m$, then $m$ is an integer multiple of $8$

steps.text: $FG = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$, so $a = 0$, $b = -1$, $c = 1$, $d = 1$.
Option A: $\frac{b+ia}{d+ic} = \frac{-1}{1+i} = \frac{-1+i}{2} \ne i$: FALSE.

Option B: $\frac{az+b}{cz+d} = \frac{-1}{z+1}$. For $z = \frac{-1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}$ (primitive cube root of unity $\omega$): $z + 1 = \frac{1+i\sqrt{3}}{2}$, so $\frac{-1}{z+1} = \frac{-2}{1+i\sqrt{3}} = \frac{-(1-i\sqrt{3})}{2} = z$: TRUE.

Option C: with $M = FG$, $M^2 = \begin{bmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$ and $M^3 = -I$, so $M$ has order 6. $M^2 = M^m \iff M^{m-2} = I \iff 6 \mid (m-2)$, i.e. $m \equiv 2 \pmod 6$. $m = 14 > 2$ satisfies this but 14 is not a multiple of 8: FALSE.

Option D: for $z = x+iy$ with $y > 0$: $\frac{-1}{z+1} = \frac{-(x+1)+iy}{(x+1)^2+y^2}$, whose imaginary part is $\frac{y}{(x+1)^2+y^2} > 0$; hence it lies in $H$: TRUE. (The Möbius map $z \mapsto -1/(z+1)$ preserves the upper half-plane.)

pitfalls: In (C), noting $m = 8$ works but missing that the condition only forces $m \equiv 2 \pmod 6$
In (D), forgetting that $z = -1$ (where the map is undefined) is real, hence not in $H$
solution.final_check: B and D true; A and C false. Key facts: $FG = [[0,-1],[1,1]]$, $(FG)^3 = -I$, $\Im(-1/(z+1)) = y/|z+1|^2 > 0$.

stem: Let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the set of all positive integers. Consider the sets $A = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ and $B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$. Let $M$ be the set of all functions $f: A \to B$ such that $f(2) \ne 2$ and $f(4) \ne 4$. Consider the set $N = \{f \in M :$ there exists a function $g: B \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $g(f(x)) = 2x$ for all $x \in A\}$. Then the number of elements in the set $N$ is _______.

steps.text: Key observation: if $g(f(x)) = 2x$ for all $x \in A$, then $f$ must be injective, because $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$ gives $2x_1 = g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)) = 2x_2$, so $x_1 = x_2$.

Conversely, if $f: A \to B$ is injective, such a $g$ always exists: define $g$ on the image of $f$ by $g(f(x)) = 2x$ (well-defined by injectivity) and extend arbitrarily to the rest of $B$ (e.g. $g(y) = 1$). Hence $N$ is exactly the set of injective $f: A \to B$ with $f(2) \ne 2$, $f(4) \ne 4$.
Count injective maps $A \to B$ ($|A| = 5$, $|B| = 7$) with the two restrictions, by inclusion--exclusion. Total injective maps: $P(7,5) = 7 \cdot 6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 2520$.

Maps with $f(2) = 2$: fix $f(2)$, injectively assign the other $4$ values from $6$ remaining: $P(6,4) = 360$. Same count, $360$, for $f(4) = 4$. Maps with both $f(2) = 2$ and $f(4) = 4$: $P(5,3) = 60$.

pitfalls: Forgetting that $g$ need only exist on the image of $f$ (no need for $f$ to be surjective)
Double-counting the overlap in inclusion--exclusion
solution.final_check: Direct alternative count: 31 admissible $(f(2),f(4))$ pairs times $P(5,3)=60$ for the rest gives $31 \times 60 = 1860$.

stem: A bookshelf contains 6 distinct books of Mathematics and 5 distinct books of Physics. From these 11 books, 6 books are chosen at random. Let $X$ be the absolute value of the difference between the number of Mathematics books chosen and the number of Physics books chosen. If $\mu$ is the mean of the random variable $X$, then the value of $77\mu$ is _______.

steps.text: Let $X_M$ be the number of Mathematics books chosen; then the number of Physics books is $6 - X_M$, so $X = |X_M - (6 - X_M)| = |2X_M - 6|$. $X_M$ ranges over $1, 2, \ldots, 6$ (at least one Mathematics book must be chosen since only $5$ Physics books exist).
$\mu = E[X] = \dfrac{4 \cdot 6 + 2 \cdot 75 + 0 \cdot 200 + 2 \cdot 150 + 4 \cdot 30 + 6 \cdot 1}{462} = \dfrac{600}{462}$.

pitfalls: Using $X = |X_M - X_P|$ directly without noting $X_P = 6 - X_M$
Forgetting $X_M \ge 1$
solution.final_check: $77 \times 600/462 = 100$ exactly, since $77 \times 600 = 46200 = 462 \times 100$.

stem: Consider a data consisting of 10 observations $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{10}$, whose mean is 5 and variance is 7. If the mean and the variance of the first 8 observations $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_8$ are 4 and 3.5, respectively, and $x_9 < x_{10}$, then the value of $3x_9 + 2x_{10}$ is _______.

steps.text: Sum of all $10$ observations: $10 \times 5 = 50$. Sum of the first $8$: $8 \times 4 = 32$. Hence $x_9 + x_{10} = 50 - 32 = 18$.

Sum of squares of all $10$: $10 \times 7 + \dfrac{50^2}{10} = 70 + 250 = 320$. Sum of squares of the first $8$: $8 \times 3.5 + \dfrac{32^2}{8} = 28 + 128 = 156$. Hence $x_9^2 + x_{10}^2 = 320 - 156 = 164$.

pitfalls: Using sample variance ($n-1$ denominator) instead of population variance
Assigning $x_9 = 10, x_{10} = 8$ despite $x_9 < x_{10}$

stem: Consider the ellipse $E$ given by $\frac{x^2}{18} + \frac{y^2}{12} = 1$. Let $H$ be the hyperbola whose eccentricity is the reciprocal of the eccentricity of $E$ and whose foci are the same as that of $E$. Let $P$ and $Q$ be the points of intersection of $H$ and the parabola $\sqrt{5}\,y = x^2$ in the first quadrant. Let $d$ be the distance between $P$ and $Q$. If $A$ and $B$ are the integers such that $d^2 = A + B\sqrt{5}$, then the value of $A - B$ is _______.

steps.text: For $E$: $a^2 = 18$, $b^2 = 12$, so $e_E = \sqrt{1 - 12/18} = \sqrt{1/3} = 1/\sqrt{3}$. The foci are at $(\pm c, 0)$ with $c = a e_E = \sqrt{18}/\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{6}$.

$H$ has eccentricity $e_H = 1/e_E = \sqrt{3}$ and the same foci, so $c^2 = 6$. For the hyperbola $x^2/a_h^2 - y^2/b_h^2 = 1$: $a_h^2 = c^2/e_H^2 = 6/3 = 2$ and $b_h^2 = c^2 - a_h^2 = 4$. Thus $H: \frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{y^2}{4} = 1$.

Intersect with $y = x^2/\sqrt{5}$: $\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^4}{20} = 1$. With $u = x^2$: $10u - u^2 = 20$, i.e. $u^2 - 10u + 20 = 0$, giving $u = 5 \pm \sqrt{5}$, both positive. In the first quadrant this yields two points $P, Q$ with $x$-coordinates $\sqrt{5+\sqrt{5}}$ and $\sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$.

Difference of $x$-coordinates: $s = \sqrt{5+\sqrt{5}} - \sqrt{5-\sqrt{5}}$, $s^2 = 10 - 2\sqrt{(5+\sqrt{5})(5-\sqrt{5})} = 10 - 2\sqrt{20} = 10 - 4\sqrt{5}$. Difference of $y$-coordinates: $\frac{(5+\sqrt{5}) - (5-\sqrt{5})}{\sqrt{5}} = 2$.

pitfalls: Taking $e_H = e_E$ instead of the reciprocal
Forgetting both roots $5 \pm \sqrt{5}$ give first-quadrant points
solution.final_check: Numerically $d^2 = 14 - 4\sqrt{5} \approx 5.056 > 0$, consistent with a genuine distance.

stem: For a real number $\alpha$, let $[\alpha]$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $\alpha$. For a finite set $M$, let $|M|$ denote the number of elements in the set $M$. Consider the functions $f: (-3, 3) \to (-\infty, \infty)$ and $g: (-3, 3) \to (-\infty, \infty)$ defined by $f(x) = [x^3]\log_e(1 + \sin^2(\pi(x - [x])))$ and $g(x) = x^3\sin^2(\pi\log_e(1 + x - [x]))$. Let $A = \{x \in (-3, 3) : f$ is discontinuous at $x\}$ and $B = \{x \in (-3, 3) : g$ is discontinuous at $x\}$. Then the value of $|A| + 2|B| - |A \cap B|$ is _______.

steps.text: Write $f(x) = [x^3] \cdot h(x)$ where $h(x) = \ln(1 + \sin^2(\pi\{x\}))$. The fractional part $\{x\}$ jumps only at integers, but $h$ is continuous everywhere: at an integer $n$, $\lim_{x \to n} h(x) = \ln(1 + \sin^2 \pi) = 0 = h(n)$ from the left (since $\{x\} \to 1$) and $0$ from the right. Moreover $h(x) = 0$ iff $\sin(\pi\{x\}) = 0$ iff $x$ is an integer, and $h(x) > 0$ otherwise.

$[x^3]$ is discontinuous exactly at $x = \sqrt[3]{m}$ for integers $m$ with $\sqrt[3]{m} \in (-3,3)$, i.e. $m \in \{-26, \ldots, 26\}$: $53$ points. At a non-integer such point, $h > 0$ is continuous and $[x^3]$ jumps by $1$, so $f$ jumps by $h > 0$: discontinuous. At an integer point, $h = 0$ and $[x^3]$ is locally bounded, so $f(x) \to 0 = f(n)$: continuous. Removing the $5$ integers $\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}$ gives $|A| = 53 - 5 = 48$.

Write $g(x) = x^3 \cdot k(x)$ with $k(x) = \sin^2(\pi \ln(1 + \{x\}))$. At a non-integer, $g$ is continuous. At an integer $n$: $k$ has left limit $\sin^2(\pi \ln 2) \ne 0$ (since $\pi \ln 2 \approx 2.18$ is not a multiple of $\pi$) and right limit/value $0$. Hence $g$ jumps by $n^3 \sin^2(\pi \ln 2)$, which is nonzero for $n \ne 0$ but zero at $n = 0$ (where $x^3 = 0$ kills the jump, $g$ continuous). So $B = \{-2, -1, 1, 2\}$, $|B| = 4$.
$A$ contains no integers while $B$ contains only integers, so $A \cap B = \varnothing$.

pitfalls: Counting $x = 0$ as a discontinuity of $g$ (the $x^3$ factor removes the jump)
Including integers in $A$

stem: The value of $n$ is _______.

steps.text: Intersections satisfy $e^{-x} = e^{-x}(\sin x + \cos x)$. Since $e^{-x} \ne 0$, this is $\sin x + \cos x = 1$, i.e. $\sqrt{2}\sin(x + \pi/4) = 1$, so $\sin(x + \pi/4) = 1/\sqrt{2}$.
Hence $x + \pi/4 = 2k\pi + \pi/4$ or $2k\pi + 3\pi/4$, giving $x = 2k\pi$ or $x = \pi/2 + 2k\pi$ for integer $k$.

In $[0, 10\pi]$: $x = 2k\pi$ gives $k = 0, \ldots, 5$ (6 values: $0, 2\pi, \ldots, 10\pi$); $x = \pi/2 + 2k\pi$ gives $k = 0, \ldots, 4$ (5 values: $\pi/2, \ldots, 17\pi/2$; $k = 5$ gives $21\pi/2 > 10\pi$).
Total $n = 6 + 5 = 11$, with $\alpha_1 = 0 < \alpha_2 = \pi/2 < \alpha_3 = 2\pi < \alpha_4 = 5\pi/2 < \cdots$.

pitfalls: Dropping the endpoint $x = 0$ or $x = 10\pi$
Missing one of the two solution families
solution.final_check: Sorted intersections: $0, \pi/2, 2\pi, 5\pi/2, 4\pi, 9\pi/2, 6\pi, 13\pi/2, 8\pi, 17\pi/2, 10\pi$ — 11 points.

stem: Let $A$ be the area of the region enclosed between the curves $C_1$, $C_2$, and the lines $x = \alpha_1$ and $x = \alpha_4$. Then the value of $\frac{1}{\pi} - \frac{\log_e(A - 2e^{-2})}{\pi}$ is _______.

formulas: $\int e^{-x}(1 - \sin x - \cos x)\,dx = e^{-x}(\cos x - 1) + C$

steps.text: From Q15, $\alpha_1 = 0$ and $\alpha_4 = 5\pi/2$. The enclosed area is $A = \int_{0}^{5\pi/2} e^{-x}\,|1 - \sin x - \cos x|\,dx$, since the curves cross at each $\alpha_i$.

Sign of $1 - \sin x - \cos x = 1 - \sqrt{2}\sin(x + \pi/4)$ on $[0, 5\pi/2]$: it vanishes at $x = 0, \pi/2, 2\pi, 5\pi/2$; it is negative on $(0, \pi/2)$ and $(2\pi, 5\pi/2)$, positive on $(\pi/2, 2\pi)$ (check e.g. $x = \pi/4, \pi, 9\pi/4$).

Then $A - 2e^{-2} \approx 0.14548 > 0$, $\log_e(A - 2e^{-2}) \approx -1.92760$, and $\frac{1}{\pi} - \frac{\log_e(A - 2e^{-2})}{\pi} = \frac{1 - \log_e(A - 2e^{-2})}{\pi} \approx 0.93193$, i.e. $0.93$ to two decimal places.

pitfalls: Integrating without the absolute value (signed areas cancel)
Misidentifying $\alpha_4$
solution.final_check: Numerically $A = 2e^{-\pi/2} + e^{-5\pi/2} \approx 0.41615$ and the required expression is $\approx 0.93193 \to 0.93$.

stem: Let $P$ be the point in the first quadrant where the given ellipses intersect. If $\theta$ is the acute angle between the tangents to the given ellipses at the point $P$, then the value of $4\tan\theta$ is _______.

steps.text: Subtracting the ellipse equations: $(x^2 + 4y^2) - (4x^2 + y^2) = 0$ gives $3y^2 = 3x^2$, so $y = x$ in the first quadrant. Adding: $5x^2 + 5y^2 = 2$, so with $y = x$: $x = y = 1/\sqrt{5}$. Thus $P = (1/\sqrt{5}, 1/\sqrt{5})$.
Tangent to $x^2 + 4y^2 = 1$ at $P$: $x/\sqrt{5} + 4y/\sqrt{5} = 1$, i.e. $x + 4y = \sqrt{5}$, slope $m_1 = -1/4$.
Tangent to $4x^2 + y^2 = 1$ at $P$: $4x/\sqrt{5} + y/\sqrt{5} = 1$, i.e. $4x + y = \sqrt{5}$, slope $m_2 = -4$.

pitfalls: Using the obtuse angle instead of the acute one
Sign error in the tangent formula

stem: If $A$ is the area of the common region that lies inside both the given ellipses, then the value of $\cot A$ is _______.

steps.text: The common region is symmetric about both axes and about $y = x$. In the first quadrant, the ellipses meet at $P = (1/\sqrt{5}, 1/\sqrt{5})$ (from Q17). For $0 \le x \le 1/\sqrt{5}$ the binding constraint is $x^2 + 4y^2 \le 1$ (i.e. $y \le \sqrt{1-x^2}/2$), and for $1/\sqrt{5} \le x \le 1/2$ it is $4x^2 + y^2 \le 1$ (i.e. $y \le \sqrt{1-4x^2}$).

First-quadrant area $= \int_{0}^{1/\sqrt{5}} \frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{2}\,dx + \int_{1/\sqrt{5}}^{1/2} \sqrt{1-4x^2}\,dx$. The first integral equals $\frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{4}\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$; the second equals $\frac{\pi}{8} - \frac{1}{10} - \frac{1}{4}\sin^{-1}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$.

Since $\sin^{-1}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$, the first-quadrant area simplifies to $\frac{1}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$. By four-fold symmetry, $A = 2\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$.

pitfalls: Using the wrong intersection point (e.g. $(1/2, 1/2)$, which lies on neither ellipse)
Forgetting the four-fold symmetry factor
solution.final_check: Check: $A = 2\sin^{-1}(1/\sqrt{5}) \approx 0.9273$ rad and $\cot(0.9273) = 0.75$ exactly.

subject: physics
stem: A metal wire of cross-sectional area $0.5\ \text{mm}^2$ and length $100\ \text{m}$ is connected across a battery of e.m.f. $2\ \text{V}$ and internal resistance $1\ \Omega$. The density, atomic mass and electrical conductivity of the metal are $6.35 \times 10^3\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$, $63.5\ \text{g/mol}$ and $2 \times 10^8\ \text{mho m}^{-1}$, respectively. Assuming one conduction electron per atom of the metal, the drift velocity (in $\text{mm s}^{-1}$) of the electrons in the wire is:\n[Take Avogadro's number as $6 \times 10^{23}$ and charge of the electron as $1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$.]

steps.text: Resistance of the wire from conductivity: $R = \dfrac{L}{\sigma A} = \dfrac{100}{(2\times 10^8)(0.5\times 10^{-6})} = \dfrac{100}{100} = 1\ \Omega$.
Current in the circuit (wire + internal resistance): $I = \dfrac{E}{R + r} = \dfrac{2}{1 + 1} = 1\ \text{A}$.

Conduction-electron number density (one per atom): $n = \dfrac{\rho}{M}N_A = \dfrac{6.35\times 10^3}{63.5\times 10^{-3}}\times 6\times 10^{23} = 10^5 \times 6\times 10^{23} = 6\times 10^{28}\ \text{m}^{-3}$.
Drift velocity: $v_d = \dfrac{I}{neA} = \dfrac{1}{(6\times 10^{28})(1.6\times 10^{-19})(0.5\times 10^{-6})} = \dfrac{1}{4.8\times 10^3} \approx 2.08\times 10^{-4}\ \text{m/s} = 0.208\ \text{mm/s}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the battery's $1\ \Omega$ internal resistance when computing the current
Using $0.5\ \text{mm}^2$ without converting to $0.5\times 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2$
Using atomic mass $63.5\ \text{g/mol}$ directly instead of $63.5\times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg/mol}$
solution.final_check: 0.208 mm/s matches option (C); $I/(neA)$ has dimensions of velocity.

subject: physics
stem: A nuclear reactor starts producing a radioactive nuclide $X$ from $t = 0$, at a constant rate of $\alpha$ per second. Each decay of $X$ produces energy $E_0$, which is utilized to heat a liquid of mass $m$ and specific heat $s$. Assuming no heat loss from the liquid and taking $\lambda$ as the decay constant of $X$, the rate of increase in the temperature of the liquid is:

options.A: $\dfrac{\alpha E_0}{ms}(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$
options.B: $\dfrac{\alpha E_0}{ms}(e^{\lambda t} - 1)$
options.C: $\dfrac{\lambda E_0}{ms}$

steps.text: Let $N(t)$ be the number of nuclei of $X$. Production at rate $\alpha$ and decay at rate $\lambda N$ give $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \alpha - \lambda N$ with $N(0) = 0$.
Solving: $\dfrac{dN}{\alpha - \lambda N} = dt \Rightarrow N(t) = \dfrac{\alpha}{\lambda}(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$.
Decays per second (activity) $= \lambda N(t) = \alpha(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$, so the heating power is $P = E_0\alpha(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$.
With no heat loss, $P = ms\,\dfrac{dT}{dt}$, hence $\dfrac{dT}{dt} = \dfrac{\alpha E_0}{ms}(1 - e^{-\lambda t})$.

pitfalls: Using the production rate $\alpha$ directly as the decay rate (misses the transient buildup)
Confusing the net rate $dN/dt = \alpha e^{-\lambda t}$ with the decay rate $\lambda N$
solution.final_check: At $t=0$ the rate is $0$ (no nuclei yet); as $t\to\infty$ it tends to $\alpha E_0/(ms)$ (secular equilibrium) — both limits physical, matching option (A).

subject: physics
stem: A beam of polychromatic light passes through a thin prism of prism angle $6^\circ$. The refractive index of the material of the prism varies with wavelength ($\lambda$) as $n(\lambda) = \alpha\lambda + \dfrac{\beta}{\lambda^2}$, where $\alpha = 3\ \mu\text{m}^{-1}$ and $\beta = 0.096\ \mu\text{m}^2$. If $\lambda_{\min}$ is the wavelength at which the angle of minimum deviation $D_m$ is smallest, then the correct value of $D_m$ at $\lambda_{\min}$ is:

concepts: Minimum deviation by a thin prism

steps.text: For a thin prism of angle $A = 6^\circ$, $D_m(\lambda) = (n(\lambda) - 1)A$. Since $A$ is constant, minimizing $D_m$ is equivalent to minimizing $n(\lambda)$.

$\dfrac{dn}{d\lambda} = \alpha - \dfrac{2\beta}{\lambda^3} = 0 \Rightarrow \lambda_{\min}^3 = \dfrac{2\beta}{\alpha} = \dfrac{0.192}{3} = 0.064$, so $\lambda_{\min} = 0.4\ \mu\text{m}$. ($d^2n/d\lambda^2 = 6\beta/\lambda^4 > 0$, confirming a minimum.)
$D_m = (1.8 - 1)\times 6^\circ = 4.8^\circ$.

pitfalls: Misreading $\beta/\lambda^2$ as $\beta\lambda^2$ (units force $\beta/\lambda^2$: $\beta$ is in $\mu\text{m}^2$)
Trying to minimize $D_m$ directly instead of noting it increases monotonically with $n$
solution.final_check: $n = 1.8 > 1$ is physical and $\lambda_{\min} = 0.4\ \mu\text{m}$ lies in the visible range; $0.8\times 6^\circ = 4.8^\circ$ matches option (B).

subject: physics
stem: A particle of mass $m$ and angular momentum $\ell$ is moving in a circular orbit of radius $r_0$ under the influence of an attractive force $\vec{F}(r) = -\dfrac{k}{r^2}\,\hat{r}$. Keeping its angular momentum $\ell$ unchanged, the particle is displaced radially by a small distance $\delta r \ll r_0$, due to which its radial distance varies periodically. The corresponding time period is:

options.A: $\dfrac{2\pi\ell^3}{mk^2}$
options.B: $2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m\ell^6}{k^4}}$
options.C: $\dfrac{2\pi\ell^3}{3mk^2}$

steps.text: Circular orbit: centripetal force $\dfrac{mv^2}{r_0} = \dfrac{\ell^2}{mr_0^3}$ balances $\dfrac{k}{r_0^2}$, giving $\ell^2 = mkr_0$, i.e. $r_0 = \dfrac{\ell^2}{mk}$.
With $\ell$ fixed, radial motion sees $U_{\text{eff}}(r) = \dfrac{\ell^2}{2mr^2} - \dfrac{k}{r}$. Then $U''_{\text{eff}}(r) = \dfrac{3\ell^2}{mr^4} - \dfrac{2k}{r^3}$.
At $r_0$, using $\ell^2 = mkr_0$: $U''_{\text{eff}}(r_0) = \dfrac{3k}{r_0^3} - \dfrac{2k}{r_0^3} = \dfrac{k}{r_0^3}$.
$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{U''_{\text{eff}}(r_0)}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{mr_0^3}{k}} = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}\left(\dfrac{\ell^2}{mk}\right)^3} = \dfrac{2\pi\ell^3}{mk^2}$.

pitfalls: Dropping the $-2k/r^3$ term when differentiating $U_{\text{eff}}$ twice
Mixing up the radial-oscillation period with the orbital period (for $1/r^2$ they coincide, but this must be derived, not assumed)
solution.final_check: Dimensions: $[\ell^3/(mk^2)] = (ML^2T^{-1})^3/[M(ML^3T^{-2})^2] = T$ ✓; also equals the orbital period $2\pi mr_0^2/\ell$, as expected for inverse-square force. Matches option (A).

subject: physics
stem: Consider two isosceles prisms 1 and 2 with prism angles $A_1$ and $A_2$ and refractive indices $n_1$ and $n_2$, respectively, as shown in the figure. The faces $a_1b_1$ and $a_2b_2$ are parallel to each other and perpendicular to the mirror $M$. If a ray of light is incident on the face $a_1c_1$ and emerges from the face $a_2c_2$, then the correct statement(s) is/are:\n[Figure: left isosceles prism 1 (apex $A_1$ at $a_1$, $n_1$) and right isosceles prism 2 (apex $A_2$ at $a_2$, $n_2$); inner faces $a_1b_1$, $a_2b_2$ are vertical, $\perp$ to the horizontal mirror $M$. Ray: incident on $a_1c_1$ at $i_1$ $\to$ refracted through prism 1 $\to$ emergent from $a_1b_1$ at $e_1$ $\to$ reflected by $M$ $\to$ incident on $a_2b_2$ at $i_2$ $\to$ refracted through prism 2 $\to$ emergent from $a_2c_2$ at $e_2$. Dashed extensions of the outer faces $a_1c_1$, $a_2c_2$ meet above at angle $\theta$.]

options.A: If both the prisms are at minimum deviation condition, then $\dfrac{n_2}{n_1} = \dfrac{\sin(A_1/2)}{\sin(A_2/2)}$.
options.B: If prism 2 is at minimum deviation condition, then $\sin i_1 = n_2\sin(A_2/2)$ is always true.
options.C: If both the prisms 1 and 2 are thin and are at minimum deviation condition with angles of deviation $\delta_{m1}$ and $\delta_{m2}$, respectively, then $\theta = \dfrac{\delta_{m1}}{2(n_1-1)} + \dfrac{\delta_{m2}}{2(n_2-1)}$.
options.D: If prism 1 is at minimum deviation condition, then $\sin i_2 = n_1\sin(A_1/2)$ is always true.

formulas: $\sin i = n\sin(A/2)$ at minimum deviation ($i = e$, $r_1 = r_2 = A/2$)
$i_2 = e_1$ (mirror: ray leaves $a_1b_1$ at $e_1$ below horizontal, reflects to $e_1$ above horizontal, strikes vertical face $a_2b_2$)

steps.text: Mirror link: the ray emerges from face $a_1b_1$ (normal horizontal) at $e_1$ below the horizontal, reflects off the horizontal mirror $M$, and meets the vertical face $a_2b_2$ at incidence $i_2 = e_1$. This holds always.

(A): Both prisms at minimum deviation give $i_1 = e_1$, $\sin i_1 = n_1\sin(A_1/2)$ and $i_2 = e_2$, $\sin i_2 = n_2\sin(A_2/2)$. With $i_1 = e_1 = i_2$, we get $n_1\sin(A_1/2) = n_2\sin(A_2/2)$, i.e. $n_2/n_1 = \sin(A_1/2)/\sin(A_2/2)$. TRUE.

(B): Prism 2 at minimum deviation gives $\sin i_2 = n_2\sin(A_2/2)$, i.e. $\sin e_1 = n_2\sin(A_2/2)$. The claim $\sin i_1 = n_2\sin(A_2/2)$ would need $i_1 = e_1$ (prism 1 also at minimum deviation), which is not given since $i_1$ is free. FALSE.

(C): For thin prisms $\delta_{m1} = (n_1-1)A_1$, $\delta_{m2} = (n_2-1)A_2$, so the claimed $\theta$ equals $A_1/2 + A_2/2$. But the dashed extensions of the outer faces meet at $\theta = A_1 + A_2$ (each outer face is tilted $A_1$, resp. $A_2$, from the vertical). FALSE.
(D): Prism 1 at minimum deviation gives $\sin e_1 = n_1\sin(A_1/2)$ (with $r_2 = A_1/2$ at the $a_1b_1$ face). Since $i_2 = e_1$ by the mirror, $\sin i_2 = n_1\sin(A_1/2)$ always. TRUE.

pitfalls: Assuming $i_1 = i_2$ directly instead of using the mirror to link $e_1$ to $i_2$
Misreading the figure angle as $\theta = (A_1+A_2)/2$ instead of $A_1 + A_2$
For (B): forgetting that minimum deviation of prism 2 alone says nothing about $i_1$
solution.final_check: With $i_2 = e_1$ from mirror symmetry, (A) follows from $i_1 = e_1 = i_2$ under both-min-deviation, and (D) from $\sin e_1 = n_1\sin(A_1/2)$; (B) needs prism 1 at min-deviation too, (C) is off by a factor 2. Answer: (A), (D).
solution.dispute_note: Our answer is (AD): the ray geometry in the printed figure supports options A and D; the key's option (C) is inconsistent with the figure — the dashed construction lines give $\theta = A_1 + A_2$, making (C)'s right-hand side $\theta/2 \ne \theta$. Two independent blind solutions agree on (AD).

stem: In a vacuum chamber, a particle of charge $1\,\mu\mathrm{C}$ and mass $1\,\mathrm{mg}$ is projected with a velocity $(\hat{i}+2\hat{j})\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ from the $XZ$ plane at time $t=0$ in an electric field of $1\hat{i}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. At $t=0.2\,\mathrm{s}$, the electric field is switched off and a magnetic field of $6\hat{j}\,\mathrm{T}$ is switched on. The acceleration due to gravity is $-10\hat{j}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. Correct option(s) is/are:

options.A: The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t=0.3\,\mathrm{s}$ is $15\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.B: The vertical distance of the particle from the $XZ$ plane at $t=0.4\,\mathrm{s}$ is $10\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.C: The radius of the trajectory of the particle for $t>0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ is $20\,\mathrm{cm}$.
options.D: The particle will be in the $XZ$ plane at $t=0.35\,\mathrm{s}$.

steps.text: Charge-to-mass ratio: $q/m = 10^{-6}/10^{-6} = 1\,\mathrm{C\,kg^{-1}}$. For $0\le t\le 0.2\,\mathrm{s}$: $\vec{a}=(q/m)\vec{E}+\vec{g}=1\hat{i}-10\hat{j}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

Velocity: $\vec{v}(t)=(1+t)\hat{i}+(2-10t)\hat{j}$. At $t=0.2$: $\vec{v}=1.2\hat{i}$ — the vertical component vanishes exactly. Position: $x=t+t^2/2$, $y=2t-5t^2$; at $t=0.2$: $x=0.22\,\mathrm{m}$, $y=0.20\,\mathrm{m}$.

For $t>0.2\,\mathrm{s}$: $\vec{B}=6\hat{j}$, no $\vec{E}$. Magnetic acceleration $=(q/m)(\vec{v}\times\vec{B})=6(v_x\hat{k}-v_z\hat{i})$ lies in the $XZ$ plane and is perpendicular to $\vec{v}_{xz}$, so $|\vec{v}_{xz}|=1.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ stays constant: uniform circular motion with $\omega_c=qB/m=6\,\mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$, radius $r=v_{xz}/\omega_c=1.2/6=0.20\,\mathrm{m}=20\,\mathrm{cm}$. Hence (C) is correct.

pitfalls: Forgetting gravity acts throughout both phases; assuming the magnetic field changes the speed (it does no work); miscomputing q/m.
solution.final_check: y(0.3)=15 cm, y(0.4)=0, y(0.35)=8.75 cm, r=mv/qB=20 cm => A and C correct.

stem: Two charges $Q_1=q$ and $Q_2=mq$ are placed at the points $P_1(a,b)$ and $P_2(ma,mb)$, respectively, in the $XY$ plane, where $a,b\ne 0$ and $m\ne 0,1$. If $V_1$ is the potential at a point in the $XY$ plane due to charge $Q_1$ and $V_2$ is the potential at that point due to charge $Q_2$. Correct statement(s) for the points at which $|V_1|=|V_2|$ is/are:

options.A: For $m=-1$, locus of these points is $ax+by=0$.
options.B: For $m=2$, the locus of these points is a circle of radius $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ centered at $\left(\frac{2}{3}a,\frac{2}{3}b\right)$.
options.C: For $m=-2$, the locus of these points is a circle of radius $2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ centered at $(2a,2b)$.
options.D: For $m=-3$, locus of these points is $3bx+3ay=0$.

concepts: Electric potential of a point charge

steps.text: $|V_1|=|V_2|$ gives $r_2=|m|r_1$ where $r_1,r_2$ are distances from $(x,y)$ to $P_1(a,b)$ and $P_2(ma,mb)$. For $|m|=1$ this is the perpendicular bisector; for $|m|\ne 1$ it is an Apollonius circle.
$m=-1$: $r_1=r_2\Rightarrow (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=(x+a)^2+(y+b)^2\Rightarrow ax+by=0$. (A) correct.

$m=2$: $r_2=2r_1\Rightarrow (x-2a)^2+(y-2b)^2=4[(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2]\Rightarrow 3x^2+3y^2-4ax-4by=0$, i.e. $x^2+y^2-\frac{4a}{3}x-\frac{4b}{3}y=0$: circle centered $(2a/3,2b/3)$ with radius $\sqrt{(2a/3)^2+(2b/3)^2}=\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. (B) correct.
$m=-2$: $|m|=2$, identical locus to $m=2$ (center $(2a/3,2b/3)$, radius $\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$), contradicting option (C)'s $2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ centered at $(2a,2b)$. (C) wrong.
$m=-3$: $r_2=3r_1\Rightarrow (x+3a)^2+(y+3b)^2=9[(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2]\Rightarrow x^2+y^2-3ax-3by=0$: an Apollonius circle (center $(3a/2,3b/2)$), not the straight line $3bx+3ay=0$. (D) wrong.

pitfalls: Dropping the absolute value on potentials (signs of charges do not matter for |V|); confusing the m=-2 case with a different radius.
solution.final_check: m=-1 -> bisector ax+by=0; m=2 -> Apollonius circle (2a/3,2b/3), r=2/3*sqrt(a^2+b^2); m=-2 identical, m=-3 a circle not a line => A, B correct.

verification.note: First blind solve (AB) missed C; second blind solve confirms key (ABC).

stem: Consider an electric dipole comprising two charges $+q$ and $-q$ each with mass $m$, separated by a fixed distance $d$ and initially at rest with its dipole moment pointing along $\hat{i}$. A uniform electric field $E\hat{j}$ is turned on at time $t=0$ and it is turned off at $t=t_f$, when the dipole moment makes an angle $\theta_f$ with $\hat{i}$. Neglecting any sources of energy loss, correct option(s) is/are:

options.A: The center of mass of the dipole is deflected towards $\hat{j}$ in the presence of the field.
options.B: If the magnitude of the final angular velocity $\omega_f=\sqrt{\frac{2qE}{md}}$, then $\theta_f=\frac{\pi}{6}$.
options.C: If $\theta_f=\pi/3$, then the change in kinetic energy of the dipole is given by $2\sqrt{3}\,qEd$.
options.D: For $\theta_f=\pi/4$, the dipole rotates around its center of mass with a constant angular velocity after $t>t_f$.

steps.text: Net force on the dipole in a uniform field: $qE\hat{j}+(-q)E\hat{j}=0$, so the center of mass experiences no force and is not deflected. (A) wrong.

Torque about CM: $\tau=pE\cos\theta$ (with $\theta$ measured from $\hat{i}$ toward $\hat{j}$), rotating the dipole from $\hat{i}$ toward $\hat{j}$. Moment of inertia about CM: $I=2\cdot m(d/2)^2=md^2/2$.

Work-energy: $\frac{1}{2}I\omega_f^2=\int_0^{\theta_f}\tau\,d\theta=pE\sin\theta_f=qEd\sin\theta_f$. With $\omega_f^2=2qE/(md)$: $\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{md^2}{2}\cdot\frac{2qE}{md}=\frac{qEd}{2}=qEd\sin\theta_f$, so $\sin\theta_f=1/2$ and $\theta_f=\pi/6$ (first crossing, $0<\theta_f\le\pi/2$). (B) correct.
For $\theta_f=\pi/3$: $\Delta K=\frac{1}{2}I\omega_f^2=qEd\sin(\pi/3)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}qEd\ne 2\sqrt{3}\,qEd$. (C) wrong.
After $t_f$ the field is off, so $\vec{\tau}=0$ and the dipole keeps rotating about its CM with constant angular velocity (no dissipation). (D) correct.

pitfalls: Thinking the CM is pulled along the field (net force is zero); using $I=md^2$ instead of $md^2/2$; sign errors in the work integral.
solution.final_check: Net F=0 kills A; (1/2)I w_f^2 = qEd sin(theta_f) gives pi/6 for given w_f (B ok), sqrt(3)/2 qEd not 2sqrt(3) qEd (C wrong), zero torque after switch-off (D ok) => B, D.

stem: Ten moles of an ideal monoatomic gas, initially in state $\mathbf{a}$ at atmospheric pressure and temperature $T_a=27^\circ\mathrm{C}$, is enclosed in a metal cylinder of volume $V_0$ fitted with a frictionless piston. The gas is suddenly compressed to state $\mathbf{b}$ with volume $V_0/3$. Now, keeping the piston stationary, the cylinder is submerged in a water bath of temperature $11^\circ\mathrm{C}$ until the gas reaches the temperature of the water bath, which is denoted as state $\mathbf{c}$. Finally, while still in the water bath, the piston is brought slowly to its initial position, which is denoted as state $\mathbf{f}$. If $R$ is universal gas constant, then the correct option(s) is/are: [Given: $9^{1/3}=2.08$]

options.A: The schematic P-V diagram of the processes described above is: [P-V axes; dashed verticals at $V_0/3$ and $V_0$; steep adiabatic curve from $\mathbf{a}$ (at $V_0$) up-left to $\mathbf{b}$ (at $V_0/3$); vertical downward arrow $\mathbf{b}\to\mathbf{c}$ (isochoric cooling); rightward-arrowed isothermal curve $\mathbf{c}\to\mathbf{f}$ ending at $V_0$ slightly below $\mathbf{a}$].
options.B: The change in internal energy in going from state $\mathbf{a}$ to $\mathbf{b}$ is $4860R$.
options.C: The net change in the internal energy in the whole process is $-240R$.
options.D: The pressure and temperature of the state $\mathbf{b}$ are $2.08$ times the atmospheric pressure and $624\,\mathrm{K}$, respectively.

steps.text: Sudden compression $\mathbf{a}\to\mathbf{b}$ is adiabatic: $T_b=T_a(V_a/V_b)^{\gamma-1}=300\times 3^{2/3}=300\times 9^{1/3}=300\times 2.08=624\,\mathrm{K}$.
$\Delta U_{a\to b}=nC_v(T_b-T_a)=10\cdot\frac{3R}{2}\cdot(624-300)=15R\times 324=4860R$. (B) correct.

State $\mathbf{c}$: $V=V_0/3$, $T_c=11^\circ\mathrm{C}=284\,\mathrm{K}$ (isochoric cooling). State $\mathbf{f}$: $V=V_0$, $T_f=284\,\mathrm{K}$ (slow = isothermal expansion in the bath). Net $\Delta U=nC_v(T_f-T_a)=15R(284-300)=-240R$. (C) correct.
$P_b/P_a=(T_b/T_a)(V_a/V_b)=2.08\times 3=6.24$, so $P_b=6.24\,P_{\mathrm{atm}}\ne 2.08\,P_{\mathrm{atm}}$. The temperature claim in (D) is right but the pressure claim is wrong, so (D) is wrong.

P-V schematic: steep adiabatic $\mathbf{a}\to\mathbf{b}$ (up-left), vertical isochore $\mathbf{b}\to\mathbf{c}$ down, isothermal $\mathbf{c}\to\mathbf{f}$ rightward at $284\,\mathrm{K}$ ending on the $V_0$ line below $\mathbf{a}$ (since $T_f<T_a$ at the same volume). Matches the given diagram. (A) correct.

pitfalls: Using $3^{5/3}$ incorrectly for the pressure ratio in (D); forgetting $T_f$ equals the bath temperature (284 K), not 300 K; treating sudden compression as isothermal.
solution.final_check: T_b=624K, dU_ab=4860R, net dU=-240R, P_b=6.24 atm not 2.08 atm, diagram matches => A, B, C correct.

stem:
Two thin wires, Wire-1 of diameter $0.650\ \mathrm{mm}$ and Wire-2 of unknown diameter $d$ are given. To obtain the value of $d$, the diameters of the two wires are measured with a screw gauge. The screw gauge has a pitch of $0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$ and there are $100$ divisions on the circular scale (CS). The smallest division on the linear scale (LS) is $0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$. The table shows the readings of LS and CS for the measurements:

Readings $-$ Wire-1: LS $= 0.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, CS $= 42$; Wire-2: LS $= 1.5\ \mathrm{mm}$, CS $= 95$.

The value of $d$ (in $\mu\mathrm{m}$) is:

steps.text: Least count $= 0.5/100 = 0.005\ \mathrm{mm} = 5\ \mu\mathrm{m}$.
Observed diameter of Wire-1 $= 0.5 + 42 \times 0.005 = 0.710\ \mathrm{mm}$. Its true value is $0.650\ \mathrm{mm}$, so the zero error is $+0.060\ \mathrm{mm}$ (the gauge reads high).
Observed diameter of Wire-2 $= 1.5 + 95 \times 0.005 = 1.975\ \mathrm{mm}$. Corrected: $1.975 - 0.060 = 1.915\ \mathrm{mm} = 1915\ \mu\mathrm{m}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the zero-error correction obtained from the known wire; sign of the correction (subtract a positive zero error).
solution.final_check: 0.71 mm observed vs 0.650 mm true gives -0.06 mm correction; 1.975 - 0.06 = 1.915 mm = 1915 um. Consistent.

stem: In a single slit diffraction experiment, a slit of width $(0.016 \pm 0.002)\ \mathrm{mm}$ is used to measure the wavelength of a monochromatic light source. In the diffraction pattern, the angular distance between the central maximum and first minimum is measured to be $(2^\circ \pm 40')$. The value of the fractional error in the measurement of wavelength is: [Given: $\sin(2^\circ) = 0.035$]

steps.text: From $a\sin\theta = \lambda$, $\Delta\lambda/\lambda = \Delta a/a + \Delta(\sin\theta)/\sin\theta$.
$\Delta\theta = 40' = (2/3)^\circ = \pi/270\ \mathrm{rad} \approx 0.01164$. So $\Delta(\sin\theta) \approx \cos 2^\circ \times 0.01164 \approx 0.01163$, and $0.01163/0.035 \approx 0.3323$.
Total fractional error $= 0.125 + 0.3323 = 0.4573 \to 0.46$ (rounded to two decimals).

pitfalls: Using degrees instead of radians for the $\Delta\theta$ term; forgetting the $\cos\theta$ factor; dropping the $\Delta a/a$ term.
solution.final_check: 0.125 + 0.3323 = 0.4573; rounding to two decimals gives 0.46 (truncation would give 0.45).

stem: As shown in the figure, a ray $AB$ of unpolarized light enters from water of refractive index $n_w = 4/3$ into a medium of refractive index $n_p = 4/\sqrt{3}$ after passing through a glass plate of refractive index $n_g = 1.5$ and a layer of water. At a particular incident angle $i$ the reflected ray $CD$ is polarized in the direction as shown in the figure (polarization perpendicular to the plane of incidence). The value of $i$ (in degrees) is:

steps.text: The reflected ray $CD$ is fully polarized perpendicular to the plane of incidence, so reflection at the water $\to$ medium interface occurs at Brewster's angle: $\tan\theta_B = n_p/n_w = (4/\sqrt{3})/(4/3) = \sqrt{3}$, hence $\theta_B = 60^\circ$ measured in water from the normal.
All interfaces are parallel, so the horizontal invariant $n\sin\theta$ is conserved: $n_w\sin i = n_w\sin\theta_B$.
Therefore $\sin i = \sin 60^\circ$ and $i = 60^\circ$.

pitfalls: Applying Brewster's law with the wrong pair of indices; forgetting that parallel slabs conserve $n\sin\theta$, making the intermediate glass layer irrelevant.
solution.final_check: tan(theta_B) = (4/sqrt3)/(4/3) = sqrt3 -> theta_B = 60 deg; slab invariant gives i = 60 deg. Exact angle.

stem: As shown in the figure, the resistance of a galvanometer $G$ can be found by the half-deflection method. A $10\ \mathrm{V}$ battery drives current through a resistor $R_1$ in series with the parallel combination of $G$ and (a variable resistor $R_2$ with key $K$). The resistance $R_2$ is adjusted such that when the key $K$ is closed the deflection in the galvanometer becomes half of the value as compared to when $K$ is open. Half-deflection is obtained at $R_2 = 4\ \Omega$ and thus the galvanometer resistance is found to be $6\ \Omega$. In this half-deflection condition the current (in $\mathrm{mA}$) through the resistor $R_1$ is:

steps.text: Let $P = G\parallel R_2 = 6\times4/10 = 2.4\ \Omega$ and the current-division factor $R_2/(G+R_2) = 0.4$.
Half-deflection: $\frac{0.4\,E}{R_1 + 2.4} = \frac{E}{2(R_1 + 6)}$. Cancelling $E$: $0.4(R_1+6) = 0.5(R_1+2.4)$, giving $R_1 = 12\ \Omega$.

In the half-deflection (key closed) condition the battery current through $R_1$ is $I = E/(R_1 + P) = 10/14.4\ \mathrm{A} = 0.69444\ \mathrm{A} = 694.44\ \mathrm{mA}$ (both rounding and truncation to two decimals give $694.44$).

pitfalls: Using $R_2 = G$ (the approximate rule) instead of the given $G = 6\ \Omega$; forgetting that closing $K$ changes the total current, so the simple $R_2 = G$ rule needs the correction solved here.
solution.final_check: R1 = 12 ohm from 0.4(R1+6) = 0.5(R1+2.4); 10/14.4 A = 694.44 mA exactly to 2 decimals under both round and truncate.

stem: In a new system of units, the units of mass, length, time and current are $5\ \mathrm{kg}$, $5\ \mathrm{m}$, $5\ \mathrm{s}$ and $5\ \mathrm{A}$, respectively. If $\mu_0$ and $\epsilon_0$ are the permeability and permittivity of free space, respectively, then in this new system of units, the magnitude of one SI unit of $\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon_0}$, is:

steps.text: $\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon_0}$ has dimensions of impedance (ohm): $[ML^2T^{-3}I^{-2}]$.

Convert $1\ \Omega_{\mathrm{SI}} = 1\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2\,s^{-3}\,A^{-2}}$ with $1\ \mathrm{kg} = M_{\mathrm{new}}/5$, $1\ \mathrm{m} = L_{\mathrm{new}}/5$, $1\ \mathrm{s} = T_{\mathrm{new}}/5$, $1\ \mathrm{A} = I_{\mathrm{new}}/5$.
Magnitude $= 5^{-1}\cdot5^{-2}\cdot5^{3}\cdot5^{2} = 5^{2} = 25$ new units.

pitfalls: Misidentifying the dimensions of $\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon_0}$; sign errors in the exponent when converting $T^{-3}$ and $I^{-2}$.
solution.final_check: Exponent: -1-2+3+2 = 2, so 5^2 = 25. Integer, exact.

stem: The height (in $\mathrm{m}$) of the liquid in the left chamber at $t = 500\ \mathrm{s}$ is:

steps.text: Each chamber has horizontal area $A_c = 1\times1 = 1\ \mathrm{m}^2$; total liquid volume $2\ \mathrm{m}^3$ gives $h_L + h_R = 2$, so the driving head is $\Delta h = h_L - h_R = 2h_L - 2$.

Torricelli: $dh_L/dt = -(A_h/A_c)\sqrt{2g(2h_L - 2)} = -(A_h/A_c)\cdot 2\sqrt{g}\sqrt{h_L - 1}$. With $A_h = \sqrt{10}\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}^2$ and $\sqrt{g} = \sqrt{10}$, $d(\sqrt{h_L-1})/dt = -10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$.
$\sqrt{h_L - 1} = 1 - 10^{-3}t$. At $t = 500\ \mathrm{s}$: $\sqrt{h_L-1} = 0.5$, so $h_L = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}$ (right chamber $0.75\ \mathrm{m}$, still above the bottom hole, consistent).

pitfalls: Using $\Delta h = h_L$ instead of $h_L - h_R$; unit error converting $\mathrm{cm}^2$ to $\mathrm{m}^2$; forgetting the hole must stay submerged (it does: $h_R = 0.75\ \mathrm{m}$).
solution.final_check: sqrt(hL-1) = 1 - 0.001*500 = 0.5 -> hL = 1.25 m; equilibrium (1 m) not yet reached. Exact.

stem: The difference in the capacitance (in $\mathrm{F}$) between the metal plates at $t = 0$ and that at $t = 500\ \mathrm{s}$ is $(8 - n)\epsilon_0$, where $\epsilon_0$ is the permittivity of free space. The value of $n$ is:

steps.text: At $t = 0$: left chamber full of $\epsilon_r = 15$ liquid: $C_L = \epsilon_0(1)(15)/2 = 7.5\epsilon_0$; right chamber air: $C_R = \epsilon_0/2 = 0.5\epsilon_0$. Total $C(0) = 8\epsilon_0$.
Difference $= (8 - 128/65)\epsilon_0$, so $n = 128/65 = 1.96923\ldots \to 1.97$ (rounded to two decimals).

pitfalls: Treating the vertical liquid/air stack as parallel instead of series; using the wrong chamber footprint area (each chamber is $1\ \mathrm{m}^2$, not $2\ \mathrm{m}^2$).

stem: After the collision the disk starts to rotate around point $C$ in the $XY$ plane. The maximum change in the height (in $\mathrm{m}$) of its center $O$ is:

concepts: Conservation of angular momentum about pivot

steps.text: Take $O$ as origin, $x$ right, $y$ up, $z$ out of page. $P$ is at $45^\circ$ on the right: $\mathbf{r}_{P/C} = (R/\sqrt{2},\,-R(1+1/\sqrt{2}))$ with $R = 0.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

Particle angular momentum about $C$: $L_{i,z} = -y_P(-100m)\cdot$... explicitly $L_{i,z} = x_P p_y - y_P p_x = -100mR(1+1/\sqrt{2}) = -0.68284\ \mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$; after: $L_{f,z} = (R/\sqrt{2})(-90m) = -0.25456$.
Disk gains $I_C\omega = L_i - L_f = -0.42828$; $I_C = 3MR^2/2 = 0.06$, so $|\omega| = 7.138\ \mathrm{rad/s}$.

pitfalls: Taking angular momentum about $O$ instead of the pivot $C$ (the pivot impulse has moment only about other points); misplacing $P$ (it is at $45^\circ$ on the right, not at the bottom or rightmost point); using $I_O$ instead of $I_C$.

subject: physics
stem: Amount of energy loss (in $\mathrm{J}$) in the collision is:

steps.text: Initial KE of particle: $\frac{1}{2}(0.02)(100)^2 = 100\ \mathrm{J}$.
Final KE of particle: $\frac{1}{2}(0.02)(90)^2 = 81\ \mathrm{J}$. Disk rotational KE from Q17: $\frac{1}{2}(0.06)(7.138)^2 = 1.5286\ \mathrm{J}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the disk's rotational KE in the balance; using $\omega$ about $O$ with $I_O$.
solution.final_check: 100 - 81 - 1.5286 = 17.4714 -> 17.47 J; round and truncate agree.
